newsitem.title: NIGERIA: Shell Nigeria says flowlines replacement on course.
newsitem.headline: Shell Nigeria says flowlines replacement on course.

text.p: Royal Dutch/Shell's Nigerian unit said the replacement programme for its swamp and land flowlines was on course and nearing completion.
Chris Haynes, technical manager of the Western Division of The Shell Petroleum Development Company of Nigeria, told visiting reporters that the programme was 95 percent complete in the area.
"We started with the replacement programme of the swamp flowlines here in 1992 and our objective is to complete it by the end of this year," he said.
"We have also made progress with those on land. This began in 1995 and we should meet the completion target of 1999."
Shell policy is to replace all flowlines that are more than 15 years old and to bury underground existing and future land flowlines.
Burying the flowlines would make them less susceptible to sabotage by aggrieved residents of the oil-producing areas, oil industry sources said.
According to Haynes, it is anticipated that by end-1996 some 225 km or 18 percent of the existing land flowlines will have been replaced and buried.
Egbert Imomoh, general manager of Shell's Eastern Division, told Reuters in the oil city of Port Harcourt that great progress had been made with the replacement policy in his area.
"I can say that for the swamp flowlines here, we've replaced above 50 percent. We're on course with the programme slowly but surely."
He did not give a figure for land flowlines replaced and buried in the Eastern Division.
Haynes said: "We are confident that at the end of the programme, there would be less leakages and spillages arising from corrosion of the pipelines."
"The programme is aimed at improving the environmental pollution problem and enhancing our assets and integrity."
Shell said on Thursday it had launched a gas gathering project, the first in a series of plans aimed at eliminating flaring by 2008.
The company has been under constant attack from residents of oil-producing areas and environmental campaigners for alleged ecological devastation.

It faced local and international pressure to shut down operations in Nigeria following the military government's hanging last November of nine minority rights activists for murder, despite worldwide appeals for clemency.
Shell currently pumps about 950,000 barrels per day (bpd) of oil, which is half of Nigerian production.
